sections.html:
Fairfield is a shoreline town in Fairfield County, bordered by Bridgeport, Trumbull, Easton, Weston and Westport. It was founded in 1639 and covers about 31 square miles, mostly land, with roughly 5 miles of Long Island Sound coastline. The 2020 census counted 61,512 residents.

Five waterways cross the town: the Mill River, Rooster River, Ash Creek, Sasco Brook and the Aspetuck River. A house a few blocks from the Sound or beside a brook is priced and insured differently from one up the hill, so ask your insurance agent which flood zone your lot is in before you settle on a price.

Fairfield's housing comes from several periods, and the period usually predicts the repair list. British troops burned much of the town on July 7, 1779, so little of the oldest building stock survives outside the historic districts around the Old Post Road and Southport.

The bigger change followed World War I. Bridgeport's munitions boom pushed workers into Fairfield, and the population grew from about 6,000 to 17,000 by 1929. The Connecticut Turnpike added another wave in the 1950s, and by the 1960s the suburban pattern was set. A house from that stretch may still have older wiring, a first-generation boiler or an oil tank, and those are what a buyer's inspector tends to flag.

Fairfield is a collection of named sections more than one uniform suburb, and buyers search by section.

  • Southport, a historic harbor village with its own rail station and library.
  • Greenfield Hill, known for large green areas, dogwood trees and a village green with a white-spired church.
  • Fairfield Beach and Sasco Hill, where new construction has changed the streets near the water and downtown.
  • Stratfield, Tunxis Hill and Grasmere.
  • Mill Plain, Knapp's Village, Melville Village, Holland Hill and Murray.

The Post Road (Route 1) and Black Rock Turnpike are the two shopping corridors. Three Metro-North stations serve the town, Fairfield-Black Rock, Fairfield and Southport, and I-95, U.S. 1 and the Merritt Parkway all cross it.

Many residents commute by rail or I-95 instead of working in town, so a house near a station draws a different buyer than one near a campus. Fairfield University and Sacred Heart University together enroll more than 17,000 students. If you own a house near either and it has a tenant, read the lease before you speak to any buyer.

Buyers with children often ask which attendance zone a house is in. The town has two public high schools, Fairfield Warde and Fairfield Ludlowe, so have your address ready when you call the Board of Education.

sections.h2: Recording a Fairfield sale and the state charge
sections.html:
A Connecticut deed cannot be recorded by the town clerk until the conveyance tax return is filed and the tax paid. Section 12-497 has the clerk record the deed only after the return prescribed by the Department of Revenue Services is filed.

Section 12-494 sets the base rates at three-quarters of one percent of the price to the state and one-fourth of one percent to the town, on conveyances of $2,000 or more. Non-residential property pays more, and so do residential sales of $800,000 or more, with tiers above $800,000 and $2.5 million. Rates have been amended over time, so confirm the current figure with your closing attorney or the Fairfield Town Clerk before relying on a number.

sections.h2: Property tax and liens to check first
sections.html:
Call the Fairfield tax collector first. The office can tell you what is owed on the current bill. Chapter 204 of the Connecticut General Statutes covers installment due dates, interest on delinquent taxes and the liens a town can file.

  • Ask for the exact payoff figure for your closing date, not an estimate.
  • Ask whether any sewer, water or other municipal charges are attached to the property.
  • Ask whether an assessment appeal or abatement is pending.

Whatever is owed is paid from your proceeds at the closing table, so a clean number up front keeps the date from slipping.

sections.h2: Listing, selling yourself or selling for cash
sections.html:
A cash buyer purchases the house as it stands, so no repairs, staging or open houses are needed. Listing can reach more buyers, but it brings inspection requests, appraisal limits and a longer calendar.

  • Listing with an agent: wider exposure, but you carry repair negotiations and showings.
  • Selling yourself: you keep the commission but handle marketing and paperwork.
  • Selling to a cash buyer: faster and simpler, usually at a price below a fully renovated sale.

Compare real offers in writing. A fair offer should survive a title search and a read by your closing attorney.

faqs.q: Is Fairfield, CT part of Fairfield County?
faqs.a: Yes. Fairfield is a town in Fairfield County on the Long Island Sound shore, bordering Bridgeport, Trumbull, Easton, Weston and Westport.

faqs.q: Do I pay a conveyance tax when I sell a house in Fairfield?
faqs.a: Connecticut taxes deeds of $2,000 or more, with part going to the state and part to the town. The rate depends on price and property type, so ask your closing attorney for the current figure.

faqs.q: Which train stations serve Fairfield, CT?
faqs.a: Three Metro-North stations: Fairfield-Black Rock, Fairfield and Southport.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Fairfield house that needs repairs?
faqs.a: Yes. Many sellers use a cash buyer for that reason, since an as-is purchase skips the repair list. Get any offer in writing and have it reviewed before you sign.

faqs.q: Who do I call about taxes owed on my Fairfield house?
faqs.a: Call the Fairfield tax collector for a payoff figure and the assessor about your assessment. Both are town offices and can confirm dates that change from year to year.
